claims.text: The hypothesis applies to nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by the balance between configurational entropy and the energy landscape of the solid solution.
The configurational-entropy/energy-landscape balance dictates defect formation and migration.
The configurational-entropy/energy-landscape balance dictates phase separation.
The configurational-entropy/energy-landscape balance dictates surface segregation.
Temperature variation over 473–1923 K changes the stability-relevant thermodynamic and kinetic behavior.
Defect formation and migration are thermally activated.
The nanoparticles will maintain structural and chemical stability up to a critical temperature.
Above the critical temperature, structural and chemical degradation will occur.
Degradation above the critical temperature is caused by increased defect formation and phase separation.
The critical temperature is expected to lie between 873 and 1273 K.
The prediction is intended to hold under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions with atmosphere and substrate interactions controlled.
Significant structural degradation or phase separation below the predicted critical temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
Maintenance of stability above the predicted critical temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
